sand.description: Pause beside the landscape where U.S. troops attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho encampment on November 29, 1864. The site preserves a place of profound loss, remembrance, and continuing importance to descendant communities.

sair.description: Explore twelve acres beside the Saugus River where seventeenth-century ironmakers brought industrial skills to colonial Massachusetts. Waterwheels, forges, and mills reveal the mechanics and labor of early iron production.

spar.description: Explore the armory landscape and collections behind nearly two centuries of military manufacturing. Firearms, historic buildings, and engineering stories reveal how Springfield influenced both national defense and American industry.

stea.description: Explore massive steam locomotives and the spaces where railroads were built, repaired, and preserved. Steamtown connects the machinery's scale with the workers and travelers who shaped the railway age.

thrb.description: Explore the Manhattan townhouse setting of Theodore Roosevelt's childhood. His early interests and efforts to overcome poor health reveal the beginnings of a lifelong enthusiasm for vigorous outdoor life.

thri.description: Visit the Buffalo house where an improvised ceremony brought Theodore Roosevelt into the presidency in 1901. The setting introduces the sudden transition and the policies that would reshape government and international affairs.

thst.description: Explore the home landscape of Thomas Stone, a Maryland signer of the Declaration of Independence. The estate connects a consequential political decision with the family and property he risked in supporting independence.

tuai.description: Explore Moton Field, where African American military pilots began their flight training during World War II. Hangars and exhibits reveal the skill and determination behind the airmen who challenged the assumptions of a segregated military.

tuin.description: Explore the campus story that Booker T. Washington began building in 1881. Historic places connect education and self-determination with George Washington Carver's agricultural research and Tuskegee's continuing influence.

ulsg.description: Explore White Haven, the Dent family home where Ulysses S. Grant met Julia and later lived with his family. The site examines their lives alongside those of the enslaved African Americans who worked the property.

vama.description: Explore a grand Hudson Valley estate built for the Vanderbilts' privileged way of life. The mansion and grounds reveal the architecture, wealth, and social world of America's Gilded Age.

waba.description: Walk the landscape where Custer's cavalry attacked Peace Chief Black Kettle's Cheyenne village at dawn on November 27, 1868. The site offers a place to remember those killed and examine the Great Plains Wars.

whmi.description: Explore the place where a mission encounter became part of a devastating transformation of Cayuse homelands. The site examines newcomers, disease, conflict, and the consequences that followed the killings of 1847.

wiho.description: Explore the hilltop Greek Revival house where William Howard Taft was born and grew up. Family rooms and stories reveal the civic values and early environment of a future president and chief justice.

cato.description: Explore wooded mountain trails in a landscape restored through New Deal-era public works. Rocky viewpoints and regrowing forest reveal how former working land became a place for recreation.

coga.description: Pause among trees, lawn, and water within the National Mall's memorial landscape. Constitution Gardens offers a quieter setting for reflection close to the capital's major monuments.

fowa.description: Explore a Potomac River fort whose defenses evolved from nineteenth-century masonry to twentieth-century concrete and steel. Its commanding riverside position reveals why this approach to Washington mattered for more than two centuries.

gree.description: Follow forest paths and camp among trees just beyond Washington's urban core. Greenbelt offers a wooded setting for walking and overnight stays close to the capital.

naca.description: Explore park places across the nation's capital, from neighborhood green spaces to landscapes tied to public memory. This retained inventory entry represents a broad park grouping rather than one entrance or visitor destination.

mall.description: Walk the capital's broad ceremonial landscape between museums, monuments, and spaces used for national gatherings. The National Mall brings commemoration, protest, and everyday public life into the same open setting.

pisc.description: Follow boardwalks over freshwater tidal wetlands and paths through meadows and woods beside the Potomac. Habitat for bald eagles, ospreys, and beavers shares the landscape with National Colonial Farm.

prwi.description: Explore wooded trails and streams in a park that began as a Depression-era recreation area in 1936. The forest connects the legacy of children's relief camps with generations of walking, cycling, and camping.

rocr.description: Explore 1,754 acres of wooded valley within the capital, protected as a federal park in 1890. Creekside paths and old trees offer a close encounter with nature and layers of human history inside the city.

whho.description: Explore the public landscape around the White House, a presidential home and a longstanding focus for protest and national debate. President's Park connects the building's familiar image with the people who have lived, worked, and gathered here.

wotr.description: Pair a performance with a park setting of wooded grounds and outdoor gathering spaces. Wolf Trap brings music, theater, and dance into a national park devoted to the performing arts.

appa.description: Follow a footpath extending more than 2,190 miles through the Appalachian Mountains, from wooded valleys to open ridges. Built by private citizens and completed in 1937, the trail offers both short walks and long-distance journeys.

cajo.description: Explore more than 3,000 miles of Chesapeake Bay water trails linking Indigenous homelands with the voyages John Smith recorded in 1608. Shoreline stops and paddling routes reveal a world of communities, waterways, and continuing Tribal connections.

iatr.description: Follow a roughly 1,200-mile route through Wisconsin's glacial landscapes. Ridges, lakes, and valleys reveal the edge of the last great ice sheet across the ancestral lands of fifteen Tribes.

lecl.description: Trace nearly 4,900 miles from Pittsburgh toward the Pacific along routes associated with the 1803–1806 Lewis and Clark expedition. Connected places reveal both the travelers' journey and the homelands of more than sixty Tribal nations.

noco.description: Explore a route of more than 4,800 miles from North Dakota to Vermont through northern forests, open prairie, and lake country. Individual trail sections reveal glacial landscapes, communities, and a remarkable variety of walking terrain.

semo.description: Trace the 54-mile route of the 1965 voting rights march from Selma to Montgomery. Interpretive places connect the roads and river crossing with the people whose nonviolent campaign challenged racial exclusion.

bicy.description: Explore more than 729,000 acres of freshwater swamp that help sustain the neighboring Everglades and coastal estuaries. Cypress country and mixed plant communities provide habitat for the endangered Florida panther.

bith.description: Explore more than 113,000 acres where longleaf pine forest, cypress-lined bayous, and other southeast Texas habitats meet. Trails and waterways reveal a biological crossroads that includes insect-eating pitcher plants and sundews.

crmp.description: Explore the wider volcanic landscape adjoining Craters of the Moon's developed monument area. Lava flows, cinder cones, and sagebrush country reveal the scale of Idaho's volcanic terrain beyond the principal visitor loop.

liri.description: Explore 15,288 acres of waterfalls, forested uplands, and sheer sandstone bluffs along a river flowing atop Lookout Mountain. Canyon overlooks and boulder-strewn pools reveal a distinctive Southern Appalachian landscape.

moja.description: Explore 1.6 million acres of Mojave Desert mountains, dunes, volcanic terrain, and Joshua tree habitat. This vast preserve also protects desert tortoises and traces of ten thousand years of human connection with the desert.

tapr.description: Walk roughly 10,900 acres of surviving tallgrass prairie in the Kansas Flint Hills, where a bison herd helps sustain the grassland. Open horizons and historic ranch places connect a rare ecosystem with generations of human use.

timu.description: Explore roughly 46,000 acres of salt marshes, coastal dunes, and hardwood hammocks with a human history reaching back some 6,000 years. Fort Caroline and Kingsley Plantation connect this estuary landscape with colonial encounter and the lives of enslaved people.

vall.description: Explore 88,900 acres of mountain meadows and meandering streams inside a volcanic depression fourteen miles wide. This ancient caldera provides habitat for elk and Gunnison's prairie dogs alongside ancestral homelands and historic ranch country.

chch.description: Explore the wooded battlefield and commanding heights where armies fought for Chattanooga in 1863. A Confederate victory at Chickamauga was followed by a Union breakthrough that opened a gateway into the South.

frsp.description: Explore four Civil War battle landscapes around Fredericksburg, Chancellorsville, the Wilderness, and Spotsylvania. Preserved fields and historic places reveal the enormous cost borne by soldiers and nearby civilians.

gett.description: Follow ridges, fields, and monuments across the landscape of the Civil War's bloodiest battle. The Union victory ended Lee's second invasion of the North and gave Abraham Lincoln the setting for the Gettysburg Address.

guco.description: Walk the wooded battlefield where Greene's and Cornwallis's armies fought on March 15, 1781. The encounter at this small courthouse community changed the course of the Revolution's Southern Campaign.

hobe.description: Explore the Tallapoosa River bend where Andrew Jackson's army attacked Red Stick Creek defenses on March 27, 1814. The battle's devastating losses and ensuing land cession reshaped the Creek homeland and the southeastern United States.

kimo.description: Follow a wooded ridge where patriot forces won an important Revolutionary victory on October 7, 1780. The battlefield reveals a turning point in the struggle for the southern colonies.

peri.description: Explore 4,400 acres where more than 23,000 soldiers fought on March 7–8, 1862. The preserved battlefield reveals a struggle for Missouri and a pivotal moment in the Civil War west of the Mississippi.

shil.description: Explore the Shiloh and Corinth battle landscapes, where the Civil War's western campaigns left a staggering human cost. Fields, woods, and preserved historic places connect military decisions with the experiences of those who fought.

vick.description: Follow the defensive landscape surrounding the Mississippi River city that both sides considered a key to victory. Fortifications and monuments reveal the campaign and siege that changed the Civil War's course.

blue.description: Explore a 10.5-mile protected reach of the Bluestone River through a rugged Appalachian gorge. Wooded slopes and riverside routes reveal a landscape rich in habitats and shaped by flowing water.

buff.description: Follow 135 miles of free-flowing river through the Ozarks, from rapids to quiet pools beneath massive bluffs. Established in 1972, Buffalo National River protects a rare undammed river landscape in the lower forty-eight states.

dela.description: Explore the Middle Delaware's forty-mile river corridor through Delaware Water Gap's wooded ridges and valley. Paddling routes and riverside stops reveal a free-flowing landscape shared by Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

losa.description: Explore the lower St. Croix's wooded riverbanks and historic river towns. This retained inventory entry covers a lower river corridor with multiple access points, rather than a single park entrance.

mnrr.description: Explore two free-flowing stretches of the Missouri that together preserve roughly one hundred miles of river country. Sandbars, banks, and broad water offer a glimpse of a river landscape transformed elsewhere by dams.

niob.description: Follow the Niobrara through a valley of waterfalls, wooded slopes, and changing habitats. Canoeing, kayaking, and riverside walks reveal an unexpectedly varied landscape within Nebraska's northern plains.

obri.description: Explore a rugged river gorge on the Cumberland Plateau, where steep sandstone walls rise above moving water. Paddling routes and overlooks reveal the meeting of rivers, rock, and forest.

ozar.description: Explore the clear, spring-fed Current and Jacks Fork rivers through the Ozark landscape. Hundreds of freshwater springs, caves, and places such as Alley Mill add depth to paddling and riverside walks.

rigr.description: Follow a 196-mile free-flowing reach of the Rio Grande through desert expanses and layered-rock canyons. Remote river journeys reveal a borderland landscape that rewards careful preparation and self-reliance.

sacn.description: Paddle through forested country along the St. Croix and Namekagon rivers, which together offer more than two hundred miles of protected riverway. Historic towns and trails create other ways to explore the banks.

upde.description: Follow the Delaware through rapids, quiet pools, rolling hills, and riverfront villages. Paddling and fishing places reveal a free-flowing river corridor shared by New York and Pennsylvania.

apis.description: Explore twenty-one Lake Superior islands and twelve miles of mainland shoreline within the Ojibwe homeland. Sea caves, beaches, and historic lighthouses give this northern archipelago its distinctive character.

piro.description: Explore Lake Superior's sculpted sandstone cliffs, beaches, waterfalls, and dunes. Inland lakes and deep forest add quieter terrain behind a shoreline continually shaped by the great lake.

slbe.description: Climb into high dune country above Lake Michigan, where bluffs rise as much as 450 feet. Beaches, forests, inland lakes, and historic farmsteads connect broad water views with a layered coastal history.

anti.description: Follow fields and lanes where twelve hours of fighting on September 17, 1862, left about 23,000 soldiers killed, wounded, or missing. The battle stopped Lee's first northern invasion and preceded Lincoln's preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

biho.description: Walk the landscape where U.S. troops attacked a sleeping nimíipuu camp in August 1877. The battlefield preserves a place of loss and remembrance for the Nez Perce people and all who were caught in the fighting.

brcr.description: Explore the crossroads associated with a Confederate victory under Nathan Bedford Forrest. The compact memorial landscape introduces a battle whose tactical result and longer-term consequences told different stories.

cowp.description: Walk a former pasturing ground where Daniel Morgan's army enveloped British forces in a decisive Revolutionary encounter. The open battlefield helps reveal how a carefully planned maneuver became a patriot victory.

fodo.description: Explore the river fortress whose surrender on February 16, 1862, brought Ulysses S. Grant national attention. The Union victory opened a route into Tennessee and quickly changed the military balance in the West.

fone.description: Explore the meadow landscape where fighting in 1754 opened the French and Indian War. The site connects a young George Washington with a larger struggle among British, French, and Indigenous powers.

kemo.description: Explore 2,965 acres of wooded mountain and preserved battlefield from the 1864 Atlanta Campaign. Trails and historic ground connect wide-ranging views with the armies' maneuvers and fighting.

mana.description: Walk the fields above Bull Run where armies fought in July 1861 and again in August 1862. The landscape reveals how the expectation of a short war gave way to repeated, costly conflict.

mono.description: Explore farms and riverbanks where outnumbered Union troops fought on July 9, 1864. Their delaying action bought time for reinforcements to reach Washington during a Confederate advance on the capital.

mocr.description: Follow the creek-side battlefield where patriot forces waited beyond a partially dismantled bridge on February 27, 1776. The brief encounter became an important early Revolutionary victory in North Carolina.

pete.description: Explore the ground of a 292-day siege that cut supplies to Petersburg and Richmond. Earthworks and separate battlefield sites reveal the campaign's immense cost and its role in the collapse of Lee's army.

rich.description: Explore battlefields, earthworks, and historic places surrounding the Confederate capital. The park connects military campaigns with the factories, hospitals, and civilian lives caught up in Richmond's wartime importance.

rira.description: Explore the landscape of the January 1813 River Raisin battles and their aftermath. The site connects a major British and Indigenous victory with the later policies of removal and assimilation imposed on Native nations.

stri.description: Walk fields and wooded ground where the Battle of Stones River began on the last day of 1862. The Union's gains came at a terrible cost to the soldiers and communities whose lives were changed here.

tupe.description: Pause at the memorial ground of the July 1864 fighting around Tupelo. The campaign involved United States Colored Troops and helped keep Confederate forces away from important Union railroads in Tennessee.

wicr.description: Explore the rolling battlefield of August 10, 1861, the first major Civil War battle west of the Mississippi. The costly Southern victory brought national attention to the conflict in Missouri.

ciro.description: Explore granite spires and rock formations that California Trail emigrants likened to a city. Climbing routes, walking paths, and historic traces connect unusual geology with the journeys of nineteenth-century travelers.

ebla.description: Walk a Salish Sea landscape of working farmland, coastal bluffs, and historic settlement. The reserve preserves the intertwined agricultural and cultural traditions of Native and Euro-American communities.

sacr.description: Look toward the island where a French expedition endured the deadly winter of 1604–1605. The mainland site interprets the settlement attempt and the Indigenous aid that helped survivors recover when spring returned.
